name: Scott's Hut, Cape Evans (Terra Nova Hut)
overview: Hut on the north shore of Cape Evans, Ross Island, 20 km north of Scott's earlier hut at Hut Point (Wikipedia).

Base of Robert Falcon Scott's British Antarctic (Terra Nova) Expedition of 1910-13. Scott and his men set out for the South Pole from here on 1 November 1911; the polar party died on the return (Antarctic Heritage Trust).

Prefabricated in London and trial-erected in Lyttelton, New Zealand, it took nine days to build and housed 25 men of the shore party; at 50 ft by 25 ft it is the largest of the Ross Sea huts (Antarctic Heritage Trust). Its walls were insulated with seaweed sewn into quilts, and a stable for nineteen ponies was added on the north wall (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Scott's Hut, Cape Evans: charity-run, close to half from the New Zealand government, with a British government grant toward its restoration

name: Shackleton's Hut, Cape Royds (Nimrod Hut)
overview: Hut on an ice-free patch of rock beside Pony Lake at Cape Royds, Ross Island (Antarctic Heritage Trust), twenty-three miles north of Hut Point (Wikipedia).

Base of Ernest Shackleton's British Antarctic (Nimrod) Expedition of 1907-09, the third British expedition to the Ross Sea in ten years. The Nimrod carried a shore party of 14 men, 15 Manchurian ponies, nine dogs and an Arrol-Johnston motorcar (Antarctic Heritage Trust).
From here a party of five made the first ascent of Mount Erebus in March 1908, and Shackleton's southern party turned back less than 97 nautical miles from the Pole (Antarctic Heritage Trust).
funding_verdict: Shackleton's Hut: charity-run, close to half from the New Zealand government, with whisky sales and a whisky brand among its backers

name: Australian Antarctic Arts Fellowship
overview: A government residency that sends artists and creative professionals in any artform to Antarctica and the sub-Antarctic to develop work shared with Australian audiences on their return (Australian Antarctic Division).
Run since 1984 as part of the Australian Antarctic Program, administered by the Australian Antarctic Division of the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (RMIT).
Fellows travel to one of Australia's research stations: Casey, Davis, Mawson or Macquarie Island (Australian Antarctic Division).
funding_verdict: Australian Antarctic Arts Fellowship: public: the Australian government's Antarctic Division, with a grant from ANAT
wider_context: The fellowship's stated aims include "demonstrating Australia's continuing connection with the region, established through its historical presence and legacy" (Australian Antarctic Division).

Australia claims about 42 per cent of Antarctica as the Australian Antarctic Territory; under the Antarctic Treaty all claims are held in abeyance, and only Norway, New Zealand, France and the United Kingdom accept Australia's claim (Wikipedia).

In April 2023 an independent review of the Antarctic Division by Leigh Russell found intentional exclusion, gender discrimination, bullying and sexual harassment; of 236 people surveyed, 15 per cent said they had been sexually harassed and 34 per cent bullied (The Canberra Times, Miriam Webber). A follow-up review completed in March 2026 found "meaningful progress" (Australian Antarctic Division).
The Division that faced these findings runs the fellowship and the stations where fellows live.

name: Esperanza Base museum
overview: A small museum inside Esperanza Base, a year-round Argentine station at Punta Foca on Hope Bay, at the north-eastern tip of the Antarctic Peninsula; the base also has a post office, a chapel, a school and the radio station LRA 36 (Ministry of Defence, 17 Dec 2023; Argentine Army).

The base was inaugurated in December 1952 as Bahía Esperanza Army Base by Captain Jorge Edgar Leal, who later commanded Operation 90 and directed the National Antarctic Directorate (Ministry of Foreign Affairs).

In 1978 the Fortín Sargento Cabral village of seven families was added; Emilio Marcos Palma, born there on 7 January 1978, was the first documented human birth in Antarctica (Ministry of Foreign Affairs). The chapel of San Francisco de Asís opened on 28 February 1976 (Ministry of Foreign Affairs).
funding_verdict: Esperanza Base museum: state: the Argentine armed forces' base, paid for by the Argentine state
wider_context: The Army states that the base's work aims "to consolidate the country's sovereignty in the Antarctic Territory and make our position known to the other countries of the world" (Argentine Army; translated from Spanish). The Ministry of Defence says it was founded to build a village of families that would consolidate Argentina's sovereign rights over its Antarctic territory (Ministry of Defence, 2023).
Argentina's Antarctic claim overlaps British and Chilean claims, and none has wide international recognition (Wikipedia).
On 1 February 1952 an Argentine Navy party fired machine guns over the heads of a British Falkland Islands Dependencies Survey team at Hope Bay; Argentina later apologised (Wikipedia).
The museum is part of the base that the state set up to back this claim.

name: Scott's Discovery Hut
overview: Prefabricated hut at Hut Point on Ross Island, by McMurdo Sound, about 300 m from the US McMurdo Station; New Zealand's Scott Base is on the same peninsula (Wikipedia).

Built in February 1902 for Robert Falcon Scott's National Antarctic (Discovery) Expedition of 1901-04, a joint venture of the Royal Geographical Society and the Royal Society (Antarctic Heritage Trust).

Prefabricated in Sydney of Douglas fir and Scots pine, square, with a verandah on three sides (Antarctic Heritage Trust); designed by Professor Gregory and made by James Moore for £870 14s 5d (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Scott's Discovery Hut: charity-run, with close to half its operator's income from the New Zealand government

name: Antarctic Artists and Writers Program (Polar STEAM)
operator: US National Science Foundation; Oregon State University
overview: A US National Science Foundation programme that takes artists and writers to Antarctica to make work that helps the public understand the continent and the science done there. The atlas places it at McMurdo Station, one of three US year-round stations (NSF).
It took shape in the 1980s after years of campaigning by NSF programme manager Guy Guthridge; by 2015 it sent one or two people a year (Pacific Standard, 2015).

Since 2022 Oregon State University has run it, together with the Polar Educators programme for teachers, under an NSF cooperative agreement called "Polar STEAM: Where Curiosity Thrives", from 1 September 2022 to 31 August 2028. The principal investigator is Kari O'Connell (NSF award 2221990).
funding_verdict: Antarctic Artists and Writers Program: wholly US federal, given as logistics in kind and run by Oregon State University under a US$4 million agreement
wider_context: The administration's fiscal 2026 budget request proposed a 70 per cent cut to polar science research and ending NSF's lease of the icebreaker Nathaniel B. Palmer; for now NSF planned to try to keep its land stations, McMurdo among them, operating (Scientific American, Douglas Fox, August 2025).

NSF announced in 2024 that it would fund no new projects for the 2024-25 and 2025-26 field seasons, and the Trump administration cancelled the construction budget for McMurdo (ExplorersWeb, April 2025).
The programme depends on the same NSF logistics, stations and polar budget.

press_items.title: Elizabeth Harrington, "Taxpayers Pay for Poets to Travel to Antarctica" (2014)

name: Port Lockroy (Base A, Bransfield House)
overview: Former British base on Goudier Island, in a sheltered harbour off Wiencke Island on the west side of the Antarctic Peninsula (UKAHT).

Set up on 11 February 1944 under Operation Tabarin, a secret wartime mission of the British Government to establish a permanent presence and assert territorial claims; it ran as an atmospheric research base and wireless hub until January 1962 (UKAHT).
Designated Historic Site and Monument no. 61 in 1995; a British Antarctic Survey team restored the buildings in 1996, and the base has been a museum since November 1996 (UKAHT).
funding_verdict: Port Lockroy: self-funded through its shop and post office, inside a charity backed by UK government bodies, trusts and cruise operators

name: Hillary's Hut (TAE/IGY Hut A), Scott Base
overview: The first building of New Zealand's Scott Base at Pram Point, at the southern tip of Ross Island, with Mount Erebus behind; it stands on the south-western edge of the base's green, flat-roofed buildings (Antarctic Heritage Trust).
Built by Sir Edmund Hillary's team in January 1957 during the Commonwealth Trans-Antarctic Expedition; it was the first New Zealand base in the Ross Dependency (New Zealand Government, 26 Nov 2016).

Scott Base was set up in the summer of 1956 to 1957 with New Zealand government support for the expedition and the International Geophysical Year; 23 men under Hillary, five of them scientists, wintered there, laying supply depots towards the South Pole for Vivian Fuchs (Antarctic Heritage Trust).
funding_verdict: Hillary's Hut: charity-run conservation: the Antarctic Heritage Trust, with New Zealand government grants and donations
wider_context: New Zealand claims the Ross Dependency; only Australia, the United Kingdom, France and Norway accept the claim, and the Antarctic Treaty holds all claims in abeyance (Wikipedia).
The Trust describes the hut's virtual tour as celebrating "New Zealand's first leadership presence in Antarctica" (Antarctic Heritage Trust).

An earlier plan to rebuild Scott Base was paused because it could not be delivered within approved funding; Cabinet approved a reset programme in May 2026, and LT McGuinness signed the construction contract in July 2026 for completion in 2030 (Antarctica New Zealand, 30 Jul 2026).
The hut stands inside the base under redevelopment and inside the territory New Zealand claims.

name: Wordie House (Base F)
overview: Small British base hut on Winter Island in the Argentine Islands, Wilhelm Archipelago, off the west coast of Graham Land (UKAHT).

The first hut, built in 1935 for the British Graham Land Expedition, was destroyed in 1946 by a suspected tsunami. The present hut went up in 1947 from repurposed corrugated tin, timber and packing crates, was used until 1954 and was briefly reoccupied in the winter of 1960 (UKAHT).
Named after the Scottish geologist James Wordie, chief scientist on Shackleton's Endurance expedition of 1914-17 and president of the Royal Geographical Society from 1951 to 1954 (UKAHT).
funding_verdict: Wordie House: charity-run, paid from the UK Antarctic Heritage Trust's general funds, which come mostly from its shops

name: Colección de Arte Amalia Lacroze de Fortabat
overview: Private art museum, branded Colección AMALITA, at Olga Cossettini 141 in Puerto Madero, Buenos Aires, with the building overlooking the northernmost dock of the district (museum website for the address, Wikipedia).

Founded by María Amalia Lacroze de Fortabat (1921 to 2012), longtime chairperson and chief stockholder of the cement maker Loma Negra, who set aside part of her own art collection for it. Opened on 22 October 2008 (Wikipedia).
Named for its founder. It is run by the Fundación Amalia Lacroze de Fortabat, which hired the Uruguayan-born architect Rafael Viñoly for the building (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Colección de Arte Amalia Lacroze de Fortabat: private: founder's foundation, money from the Loma Negra cement fortune
wider_context: History, concerning Loma Negra under the dictatorship that began in 1976, before the 2005 sale: Horacio Verbitsky, "Microeconomía del terror" (Página/12, 25 May 2014; subtitle in my translation: "Loma Negra and the tangible reasons for its support of the 1976 coup"), reports a preliminary study by the Procuración General de la Nación's economic investigation office (OFINEC), based on 118 Loma Negra account books for 1975 to 1983. Verbitsky describes the company as then owned by Fortabat. The study found that labour costs fell from 21% to 14% of the company's costs and expenses between 1976 and 1977, that taxes fell from 8% of sales in 1975/76 to 3% in 1982/83, and that profits peaked in the year that closed on 31 March 1981.

History: the same article says the labour lawyer Carlos Alberto Moreno, who defended Loma Negra's mine workers and won lawsuits against the company over occupational illness, was murdered in May 1977. It reports that in 2012 the Tribunal Oral Federal de Mar del Plata, sitting in Tandil, sentenced the retired colonels Julio Tommasi and Roque Pappalardo and the non-commissioned officer José Luis Ojeda to life imprisonment, and that the ruling included an order to investigate the board of Loma Negra.

History: the Boston Globe obituary, "Amalia Lacroze de Fortabat, Argentine patroness of art; at 90" (2012), says the Loma Negra cement businesses flourished through government contracts with the military junta.

Fortabat controlled Loma Negra until she sold it in 2005, and she created the foundation that runs the museum, which opened in 2008. These points concern the company in the 1970s, not the foundation's funding today.

name: Museo Casa sobre el Arroyo (Casa del Puente)
overview: Municipal house museum at Quintana 3900 in Mar del Plata, on grounds of natural area crossed by the Las Chacras stream (La Nación, El Economista).

Designed by Amancio Williams and Delfina Gálvez Bunge for his father, the musician and composer Alberto Williams. El Economista dates the commission to 1943, and the "Iconic Houses" network (iconichouses.org) dates the design to 1942 and completion to 1945.
Also called Casa del Puente, after the large curved arch known as "El Puente" that carries the house over the stream (El Economista).
funding_verdict: Museo Casa sobre el Arroyo (Casa del Puente): mainly public: the national government bought the house and paid for the restoration, and the Mar del Plata municipality holds it

name: ACCA
overview: Contemporary art gallery at 111 Sturt Street, Southbank, in the Melbourne Arts Precinct (stated by ACCA).
Established in 1983 and moved in 2002 into its purpose-built building (stated by ACCA).

Building: designed by Wood Marsh and completed in 2002, with four large gallery spaces and a rusty steel facade. The complex also includes facilities for the Chunky Move dance company and Malthouse Theatre. It won a RAIA Institutional Architecture Award in 2003 (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: ACCA: mainly public with philanthropic and corporate partners: Victorian, Australian and Melbourne governments, plus the Ian Potter Foundation

name: Boyd House II (Robin Boyd Foundation)
overview: House museum and headquarters of the Robin Boyd Foundation at 290 Walsh Street, South Yarra, Melbourne (robinboyd.org.au, Architecture AU).

Robin Boyd designed it in 1958 as his family home and the Boyds moved in a year later. The Foundation was established in 2004 with support from the Boyd family and the National Trust of Australia (Victoria) (Wikipedia, robinboyd.org.au).
Also called Walsh Street House and Robin Boyd House II, after its street and its architect (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Boyd House II (Robin Boyd Foundation): charity income from donors, partners, events and tours, with the house held on two callable loans

name: PICA Perth
overview: Perth Institute of Contemporary Arts, a contemporary visual and performance arts venue at 51 James Street in the Perth Cultural Centre, Western Australia.
PICA began operating from the James Street building in 1988, and the building was officially opened as PICA on 8 November 1991 (Wikipedia).

The building dates from 1896 and was the Perth Boys' and Girls' School, later a technical college annexe. It is a Federation Free Classical building on the State Register of Heritage Places (Wikipedia). Donaldson and Warn designed the conversion (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: PICA Perth: mainly public with private donors: Western Australian and federal governments, Lotterywest, City of Perth, Minderoo Foundation and individual donors
wider_context: Wikipedia says the Forrests gave A$5 billion of Fortescue shares to Minderoo Foundation in 2023.

On 12 May 2026 the Federal Court ordered Fortescue to pay the Yindjibarndi Ngurra Aboriginal Corporation A$150 million for cultural loss and A$100,000 for economic loss; the Yindjibarndi had sought A$1.8 billion (The Canberra Times, Aaron Bunch, 12 May 2026). ArtAsiaPacific (Kalani Ko, 15 May 2026) reports that Justice Stephen Burley found Fortescue's Solomon Hub operations proceeded without the consent of traditional owners.

Wikipedia describes Minderoo Foundation as founded by Andrew and Nicola Forrest, and The Canberra Times calls Fortescue "Andrew Forrest's Fortescue Metals Group". Minderoo supports PICA's Hatched program and two staff roles (PICA Annual Report 2024).

name: Bundanon
overview: Art museum, heritage homestead and artist residency site in the Shoalhaven region of the New South Wales South Coast, set across 1,000 hectares of wildlife refuge. The site is about 25 km by car from Nowra (Bundanon).

Painter Arthur Boyd and his wife Yvonne Boyd, gave the property and their art collection to the Australian people. Prime Minister Paul Keating announced the government's acceptance in January 1993, and the government set up trustees to run the Bundanon Trust (Wikipedia).
The Boyds bought Bundanon in 1979. The homestead was completed in 1866 (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Bundanon: mainly public: Australian Government, NSW Government, with a patron program of individuals and family foundations

press_items.title: John McDonald, "Bundanon: Impulse to Action" (7 May 2022; read on McDonald's own site)

name: Rose Seidler House
overview: House museum at 69 to 71 Clissold Road in Wahroonga, in Sydney's Ku-ring-gai area (Wikipedia, Time Out).
Designed by Harry Seidler for his parents, Rose and Max Seidler. Built from 1948 to 1950 (Wikipedia).
Named for Rose Seidler, who started the commission and made the main client decisions (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Rose Seidler House: public: owned by the NSW Government and run by Museums of History NSW

name: TarraWarra Museum of Art
aliases: tarrawarra museum of art yarra valley
overview: Art museum at 313 Healesville-Yarra Glen Road, Healesville, in the Yarra Valley, about 45 km north-east of Melbourne (twma.com.au, Wikipedia).

Founded by the philanthropists Eva Besen AO and Marc Besen AC, who gave the museum and about 600 works of Australian art from their collection. It was registered in 2000, launched by Prime Minister John Howard on 24 April 2002 in a temporary North Melbourne space, and the purpose-built museum opened in 2003 (Wikipedia). Wikipedia calls it the first art museum in Australia supported by a significant private endowment.

Building: the gallery was designed by Alan Powell of Powell & Glenn (Wikipedia). The Eva and Marc Besen Centre, with visible art storage and learning and performance spaces, was designed by Kerstin Thompson Architects and opened on 8 March 2025 (twma.com.au).
funding_verdict: TarraWarra Museum of Art: private: the Besen family's endowment and foundation, with corporate sponsors and some state and local government education money
wider_context: Matt Chun and Muhib Nabulsi (Matt Chun's Newsletter on Substack, 15 December 2023, an advocacy piece) argue that arts organisations receiving Besen money should divest and that the foundation "must be comprehensively rejected". Unverified: its claims that the family funded settlement expansion in the Naqab and worked with the Jewish National Fund, from that partisan source, which carries no response from the family.

It names NGV, Collingwood Yards, Polyglot Theatre, ACMI, Rising Festival and others as places where "Besen money can also be found", without amounts; its only line on the museum calls it "Besen Family owned and controlled".

press_items.title: Anita Pisch, "Tarrawarra Biennial underwhelms rather than energises" (2018)

name: Domenig Steinhaus
overview: Architect's own house at Uferweg 31 in Steindorf am Ossiacher See, Carinthia, with private lake access and a 10-minute walk from the Steindorf/Ossiacher See station (domenigsteinhaus.at).

Günther Domenig built it from 1982 to 2008 and died on 15 June 2012. In 2008 he put the house and his artistic, legal and material estate into a foundation naming Land Kärnten as beneficiary (German Wikipedia, domenigsteinhaus.at).
It carries its architect's name, and German Wikipedia calls it his "persönliches Opus magnum" (personal magnum opus, my translation).
funding_verdict: Domenig Steinhaus: mainly public: subsidies from Land Kärnten and the federal arts ministry, with in-kind help from a municipality and a school

name: Haus Wittgenstein (Bulgarian Cultural Institute)
overview: Villa at Kundmanngasse 19 in Vienna's 3rd district, Landstraße, with the institute's entrance at Parkgasse 18 (Wien Geschichte Wiki, institute website).

Built as a town house for Margaret Stonborough-Wittgenstein, who commissioned Paul Engelmann in 1925; her brother Ludwig Wittgenstein co-signed the plans approved in November 1926 and then took over all the detailed design, and the family moved in at the end of 1928 (institute website, Wien Geschichte Wiki).
Also known as the Stonborough House and the Wittgenstein House (English Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Haus Wittgenstein (Bulgarian Cultural Institute): state-funded: the Bulgarian state owns the house and its Ministry of Culture pays for and runs the institute

name: Margarete Schütte-Lihotzky Zentrum
overview: Museum and research centre in the architect's last flat, at Franzensgasse 16/40 in Vienna's 5th district; the centre calls it the only architect's flat open to the public in Vienna (centre website).
Named for Margarete Schütte-Lihotzky (1897 to 2000), who moved in at the age of 70 and lived there for 30 years (ORF Wien, centre website).
The flat and its furnishings were listed as a monument in 2021 and the museum opened in 2022; the centre has belonged to the Iconic Houses network since December 2022 (centre website).
funding_verdict: Margarete Schütte-Lihotzky Zentrum: mainly public, plus donations and in 2021 the building owner Wertinvest
wider_context: Heumarkt: Vienna's historic centre was on UNESCO's list of World Heritage in Danger from 2017 because of the Heumarkt project of Michael Tojner and his Wertinvest; the World Heritage Committee removed it on 27 July 2026, although its advisory body ICOMOS had recommended keeping it on. The tower has shrunk from a planned 73 metres to 49.95 metres and still needs an environmental impact assessment (vienna.at).

In April 2014 members of the Architekturinitiative Wien, including Friedrich Achleitner and Gustav Peichl, wrote to planning councillor Maria Vassilakou that the Heumarkt project took public space in breach of the competition brief and that a luxury residential tower could not be justified there (ORF Wien, 2014).

Fraud investigation: after a complaint by Land Burgenland, the WKStA anti-corruption prosecutors investigated Tojner, 15 other people and eight companies over the loss of non-profit status of the housing companies Gesfö, Riedenhof and Pannonia, on suspicion of serious fraud and breach of trust; his lawyer rejected all accusations (ORF Wien, June 2019). Industriemagazin counted 16 individuals and nine companies and reported searches at about 50 sites.

In May 2026 the WKStA dropped its cases against nine people and the auditor KPMG Austria but still investigates 13 suspects; Burgenland puts its damage at 163 million euros, and Tojner denies the accusations (trend, 8 May 2026).

Unverified: in 2018 Greens club chairman David Ellensohn filed a fraud complaint alleging that non-profit flats built by Gesfö were let to tourists through a company part-owned by Wertinvest; this is a party politician's complaint, and Wertinvest called the letting "rechtlich einwandfrei" (my translation: legally sound) (ORF Wien).
Wertinvest owns the centre's building and backed its 2021 restoration.
